# Week 6, Day 5.1 - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Pipelines are written in YAML or Groovy, not TypeScript - so the
prerequisite is reading two file formats.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `Deno.Command`, exit codes | [day3_1](/learn/w6/d3/p1) |
| `package.json` scripts | [day4_1](/learn/w6/d4/p1) |
| Objects and nesting | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |

**Next:** [Day 5.2 - Pipelines](/learn/w6/d5/p2)

## YAML in ninety seconds YAML is a nested object where **indentation is the nesting**. Two spaces, never tabs. | YAML | The object it means | |---|---| | `name: ci` | `{ name: "ci" }` | | `on:`
` push:` | `{ on: { push: {} } }` | | `- uses: actions/checkout@v4` | an **array** entry: `[{ uses: "..." }]` | A leading `-` means "another item in a list". Steps are a list; that is why every step starts with one.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
**Next:** [Day 5.2 - Pipelines](/learn/w6/d5/p2)

# Week 6, Day 5.2 - Pipelines

Day 4's jobs still needed a human to press **Build Now**. A pipeline removes the human: the
developer's deploy and your tests become one sequence, and yours runs because theirs finished.

> **Mode: read-and-compare.** Jenkins is not installed here, so the Jenkinsfile is **authored,
> never executed** - and labelled as such. The commands inside it are the ones
> [day4_2](/learn/w6/d4/p2) ran.

## What "pipeline" buys

| | A job someone presses | A pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Starts because | a human decided | a deploy finished |
| Weekend hotfix at 11pm | waits for you | already ran |
| Developer depends on you | **yes** | no |

The session's framing is the right one: the developer keeps your repo URL and your three
commands, and hooks them into *their* deploy. Nobody waits for anybody.

## Stages

A pipeline is a list of named stages, and the report shows you which one failed:

| Stage | Who owns it |
|---|---|
| **Build / Deploy** | developers - put the new code somewhere |
| **Test** | you - run against what they deployed |
| **Post** | reports, artefacts, notifications |

Your part is one stage in the middle. That is the whole mental model.

Three details in that file that cost real people real hours:

| Detail | Why |
|---|---|
| `bat`, not `sh` | the UI samples assume Linux. On Windows `sh` fails with *Cannot run program sh* |
| No `tools { maven ... }` | copied from a Java sample; a Node project has no Maven, and the build fails **before** it starts |
| No `junit` in `post` | Playwright writes an HTML report, not JUnit XML - unless you configure that reporter |

`node { }` here is the scripted form; `pipeline { agent any ... }` is the declarative form, shown
at the bottom of the file. Both mean *any free machine*.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The same pipeline, somewhere it can actually run

Jenkins is a server you maintain. The hosted equivalents need no server at all, and Playwright's
own docs ship ready-made configs for each - GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, CircleCI,
Bitbucket, Docker.

They differ in syntax and **not** in content: install Node, install packages, install browsers,
run the suite.

| Jenkins | GitHub Actions | Same idea |
|---|---|---|
| Job | `job` | a unit of work |
| Build step | `step` with `run:` | a command |
| SCM → Git | `actions/checkout@v4` | fetch the code |
| Build Now | `workflow_dispatch` | a manual trigger |
| Custom workspace | *(none needed)* | the runner clones for you |
| Console Output | the log view | what happened |
| Agent you maintain | `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` | the machine |

Two rows carry the real difference:

- **`actions/setup-node`** - a cloud runner has no Node. Neither does a fresh Jenkins agent; you
  installed it by hand there.
- **`upload-artifact`** - Jenkins keeps its workspace, so the report is still on disk. A cloud
  runner is **destroyed** at the end of the job. Without that step the report is gone.

A tab check and five key names catch most broken workflows before a push burns CI minutes. The
branch line matters just as much: `branches: [master]` on a `main` repo produces a workflow that
never runs and never complains.

## Why it is not installed

That file sits in `week6/generated/`, not `.github/workflows/`. Dropping a workflow into the
latter makes it run on **every push** - a decision a lesson should not make for you. To switch it
on:

```bash
cp week6/generated/day5-github-actions.yml .github/workflows/week6.yml
```

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| `sh` on a Windows agent | *Cannot run program sh* |
| A `tools` block from a Java sample | fails before the first command |
| `branches: [master]` on a `main` repo | the workflow never triggers |
| No artefact upload | green or red, and no report either way |
| `npm install` instead of `npm ci` | versions drift from the lockfile; CI stops being repeatable |

**Next:** [Day 5.3 - How this goes wrong in a real repo](/learn/w6/d5/p3)

# Week 6, Day 5.3 - How this goes wrong in a real repo

The best worked example of CI rot is in this repository, committed and broken.

## Three workflows nobody runs

`.github/workflows/` holds `ci.yml`, `e2e.yml` and `e2e-sharded.yml`, written for a version of
this course that was deleted. Every file they reference is gone.

Every one. Those workflows would fail on the next push to `main` - not because a test broke, but
because the files they name no longer exist.

| Symptom | What it teaches |
|---|---|
| References `week8/day5.ipynb` | week8 is `day1_1`-`day3_4`; the file never came back |
| References `week7/playwright.config.ts` | there is no week7 |
| Header claims the repo "is not a git repository and has no GitHub remote" | it is, and it has one |
| Three workflows on every push | three times the minutes, three things to rot |

## The lesson

A CI file is **code that nobody reads until it fails.** It rots more quietly than a test, because
a broken test shouts on your laptop and a broken workflow only shouts on a server you are not
watching.

| Habit | Why |
|---|---|
| One workflow, not three | three is three times the rot and the minutes |
| Delete workflows for deleted code | history keeps them if you need them back |
| Reference paths that exist - check in review | a renamed folder silently breaks CI |
| Read the run log after a rename | the only place the breakage shows |
| Comments describe **now** | a stale comment is worse than none |

## Self-hosted or hosted

The session's closing point, and it is the right one to end on:

| | Jenkins you run | Hosted (Actions, Azure, GitLab) |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | install, patch, back up | none |
| Parallel machines | what you own | as many as you pay for |
| Access | your network | anywhere |
| Cost | a machine plus your time | per minute |
| Full control of the box | **yes** | no |

The direction of travel is towards hosted, for the reason the session gives: **one machine cannot
run ten suites at once**, and maintaining ten machines is somebody's whole job.

Jenkins is still worth knowing. Plenty of enterprises run it, and the model - job, workspace,
step, exit code - is the same everywhere.

## Sharding, when one machine is not enough

The mechanism you would reach for next, and the repo's stale `e2e-sharded.yml` was built around
it:

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3]
steps:
  - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/3
```

Three machines, a third of the tests each, then `npx playwright merge-reports` to get one report.
That is the answer to "the regression suite takes 40 minutes" - and it needs hosted runners,
which is why it is the argument that usually ends the Jenkins conversation.

**Next:** [Day 5.4 - Practice](/learn/w6/d5/p4)

# Week 6, Day 5.4 - Practice

The last three close out the week rather than the day.

## Week 6 done

| Day | You can now |
|---|---|
| 1 | apply page objects to a second app, and replace twelve methods with one `switch` |
| 2 | say exactly which assertions a page object may own, and prove a message is invariant |
| 3 | create, commit, push, pull - and explain a rejected push |
| 4 | run a suite from Jenkins, and name your suites so the CI job never changes |
| 5 | read and write a pipeline, and spot CI that has rotted |

Every claim in these lessons was run except the Jenkins UI steps and the Jenkinsfile, which are
labelled where they appear.

problems.statement:
**Read the broken workflows yourself**
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and list what it expects that does not exist.

**Right when:** your list matches the cell in [day5_3](/learn/w6/d5/p3), and you can say what would
appear in the Actions tab on the next push.

**Write a workflow for week 6**
Author a workflow that runs `npm run test:week6` on pull requests only.

**Right when:** it parses as YAML, and you can say why `pull_request` is a better trigger than
`push` for a suite that takes minutes.

**Turn one on, for real**
Copy your workflow into `.github/workflows/`, push it to a branch of **your own** fork, and open
a PR.

**Right when:** it runs, and you can find the report in the artefacts. If it fails, fix it - a
first CI failure is the exercise.

**Cause the classic failures**
Deliberately, one at a time: `sh` on a Windows agent, `branches: [master]` on a `main` repo, and
no `setup-node` step.

**Right when:** you can match each symptom to its cause without looking them up again.

**Shard it**
Convert your workflow to three shards with a merged report.

**Right when:** three legs run, each reports roughly a third of the tests, and one report comes
out at the end.

**Translate the Jenkinsfile**
Rewrite `day5-Jenkinsfile` as a **declarative** pipeline with an extra `Lint` stage that runs
`npx tsc --noEmit`.

**Right when:** the stages are in an order you can defend, and you can say what the build should
do if `Lint` fails.

**Clean up after the course**
Decide what you would do with the three stale workflows, and write two sentences arguing for it.

**Right when:** your answer says what happens to the ideas in them, not just to the files.
